prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which established the incretin axis as a basis for treating type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B006 remains the one candidate where originality, mechanistic clarity, independent confirmation and scale of medical consequence are all at the top level, and no member has argued that it is premature. The arc runs from proglucagon processing and the identity of the truncated active peptide, through the glucose-dependent insulinotropic action in humans and the receptor biology and tissue actions, to therapies with randomized outcome evidence in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. After the full first-round exchange I keep Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The prize is for a discovery, and the discrete, citable discoveries in this chain are the human incretin physiology, the receptor and tissue biology, and the identification and synthesis of the active form. The citation can say that this knowledge made the therapies possible without claiming the whole therapeutic chain. I have not changed my preferred configuration since round 1. What round 1 changed is my view of how the omissions must be handled: the committee's rationale should state openly that Knudsen and Habener are not credited and why, so that the choice reads as a principle and not as an oversight.
statement.case_against: Credit is still the weak point and nothing in round 1 resolved it. Knudsen's acylated analogues are what produced liraglutide and semaglutide, so a physiology-centred trio can be read as honouring the hormone while skipping the step that reached patients. Habener's absence from the supplied names makes a Mojsov credit harder to defend as a clean priority statement, and Wahren-Herlenius is right that naming one without the other leaves the peptide-identification chapter exposed. I cannot adjudicate the Mojsov and Habener question from the ballots, and the chair cannot supply documents the committee does not have. If the committee decided that the active-peptide record is too uncertain to credit, I would accept Drucker, Holst and Knudsen with a citation that names physiology and translation, but I would not call that the stronger configuration. The three-person cap also means that any second prize part would require dropping one B006 name, and I do not see a candidate whose case is strong enough to justify that this year.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius moved off Mojsov in round 1 because naming Mojsov without Habener makes the peptide-identification chapter hard to defend, and she prefers Drucker, Holst and Knudsen with a citation that names both physiology and long-acting therapy.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my trio and I take it seriously. If the prize rested on a priority claim for the first identification of GLP-1(7-36), the absence of Habener would be a real flaw. I read Mojsov's credit differently: the identification and synthesis of the active form is a discrete step that made the physiology interpretable, and the citation can be worded around the active form without declaring a first. I still disagree on replacing her with Knudsen, because that would put one company scientist in the slot for a collective industrial programme, while a discovery citation can acknowledge translation in its wording. I do agree that the rationale must name the omission of Habener openly.

responses.point: El-Manira argues that crediting Knudsen requires the committee to state its translation principle openly, because the same standard bears on B004 and B040, where discovery and industrial or clinical development are mixed.
responses.response: I accept the consistency point and it is the right test. My principle is that Physiology or Medicine rewards the discovery of the biological principle and of the molecular entity or tool, and that citations may state the therapeutic consequence without crediting the engineering. Applied consistently, it does not exclude B004, where June, Sadelain and Rosenberg are credited for a conceptual and clinical proof of concept, but it does make me cautious about B040, where the credit is closer to drug development. It also means my disagreement with El-Manira on Knudsen is about this principle and not about her contribution, which I regard as essential to the drug class. I would not change the principle only because the translational step is large.

responses.point: Linnarsson holds that a physiology-centred prize with three names best protects the science, and asks the committee to state clearly that the omission of Knudsen and Habener is deliberate. He would accept Knudsen over Mojsov only if the active-peptide record proved too uncertain to credit.
responses.response: I agree with the trio and with the request. I would put the omission in the committee's rationale and keep the citation itself limited to physiology and the active form. I also accept his condition: the case for Mojsov rests on a verifiable record, and if the committee found that record too uncertain it should say so and switch. My view in round 1 was that the committee needs documentary evidence on the Mojsov and Habener question. I now think that cannot be resolved inside this discussion, so the committee should vote on the evidence it has, which supports crediting the identification and synthesis of the active form.

responses.point: Perlmann says a second part such as B039 would force the removal of a B006 laureate and drop the translational part, and he treats B039 as a strong second-tier alternative and not as a competitor for this year's main prize.
responses.response: I agree with this reading. The B039 attribution to Mori and Walter is clean, but a two-part prize would take B006 to Drucker and Holst, and I think that weakens the central discovery chain by removing the identification of the active form. I have therefore moved B039 into my alternatives, ahead of B028 and B037, while keeping B004 second. My reservation on B039 is unchanged: its clinical and physiological consequence is still developing, and Ron, Kaufman and the other UPR arms are not trivially excluded. I would take it up in a later year, or this year only if the committee wanted a second part and agreed which B006 name to drop.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen should hold the third B006 place, and whether Habener's absence changes the answer; I am relying on recalled history and not on primary documents.

Whether the committee will accept a physiology-centred citation with an explicit statement that Knudsen and Habener are not credited, or will want the citation itself to name long-acting therapy development.
For B004, whether Eshhar's omission and the Rosenberg question can ever be settled within a three-name configuration.
Whether a second prize part, such as B039, would be better kept for a later year, since it would require dropping a B006 name.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. I have no documented connection to any credited name for B006, B039 or B004. My documented ties are to Paul Greengard (postdoctoral supervisor) and about twenty co-authored works with fellow committee member Thomas Perlmann on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy. None of the shortlisted credited names appears connected to these ties. I remain open to recusal guidance if a neuroscience candidate such as B037 becomes the leading choice.
